**UKMLA IMPROVEMENT PROJECT**

do you have ideas to improve it to help candidate to the best possible
extent inline with gmc regulations filling the gaps in market and to
compete with rivals?

I've looked at the live AMaC UKMLA page, the current GMC material, and
what competing UKMLA platforms are now offering. My view is that **AMaC
has a potentially very strong position, but the next step should be to
turn the existing large amount of content into a much clearer "candidate
success system."**

The timing is particularly important because the **revised GMC MLA
content map applies to assessments from September 2026 onward** and is
explicitly a live document. The GMC says the MLA is built around **safe
practice, managing uncertainty, and holistic person-centred care**.
([General Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/education/medical-licensing-assessment/mla-content-map?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**1. First: AMaC is already stronger than the page makes it look**

Your current page claims:

-   **10,953 AKT questions**

-   **293 CPSA stations**

-   105 CPSA Master Cards

-   1,302 CPSA flashcards

-   222 Instant Fail Atlas cards

-   examination/ECG/ABG/DVLA/antibiotic/ethics/prescribing references

-   NHS language and documentation coaches

-   SBAR generator

-   consultation frameworks

-   recovery scripts

-   spoken OSCE trainer

-   actor-trap simulator

-   study planner

-   failure diagnostic

-   exam-day card. ([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html))

That is **a lot**.

In fact, I think one of your biggest problems currently is that a
candidate visiting the page can see *many resources*, but doesn\'t
immediately understand:

**"If I use AMaC, exactly how will this take me from where I am now to
being ready for my UKMLA?"**

That should become the central proposition.

**2. The biggest strategic opportunity**

I would position AMaC as:

**The UKMLA preparation system that tells you what to study, makes you
practise it, identifies why you\'re failing, and trains you to perform
safely under exam pressure.**

Not:

"We have 10,953 questions."

Because competitors can compete on question numbers.

For example, PassMedicine is reported as having 11,000+ questions, while
other competitors emphasise thousands of questions, flashcards, AI
tutors, adaptive learning and mocks.
([iatroX](https://www.iatrox.com/blog/best-ukmla-question-banks-2026?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**Question volume is becoming a commodity.**

Your differentiator should be:

**"Know what you need. Practise it. Understand your mistakes. Fix them.
Prove you\'re ready."**

That is much harder for a competitor to copy.

**3. The single most important addition: a real GMC Content Map
dashboard**

This is probably the biggest product opportunity.

The GMC says the content map is the framework for both the AKT and CPSA,
and that it covers the core knowledge, skills and behaviours needed for
UK practice. ([General Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/education/medical-licensing-assessment/mla-content-map?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Your page already says:

"The GMC lists 429 conditions and 220 presentations. Every AKT question
is linked to them, so you can track which ones you have practised."

That is good.

But I would take this **much further**.

**Candidate dashboard:**

**MY UKMLA READINESS**

  ---------------------------- --------------- --------------- ------------
  Cardiovascular               94%             78%             🟠

That transforms AMaC from a **question bank** into a **personal tutor**.

Competitors are already moving in this direction. UKMLARevisions, for
example, advertises content-map coverage dashboards and weakness-based
mocks.
([UKMLARevisions](https://ukmlarevisions.com/features/mla-content-map?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

So I would make this a priority rather than a future luxury.

**4. Build a genuine "Am I ready?" score**

This could be extremely powerful commercially.

Instead of:

"You\'ve answered 4,326 questions."

show:

And break it down:

**Knowledge:** 86%\

**8. Your "uncertainty" material could become a major AMaC USP**

This is particularly interesting.

The GMC specifically identifies **managing uncertainty** as one of the
three overarching MLA themes. ([General Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/cdn/documents/251015---mla-content-map--english-_pdf-112647970.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Most question banks essentially train:

"What is the diagnosis?"

But real clinical reasoning often involves:

"You don\'t know yet. What should you do next?"

You could create a dedicated:

**UKMLA Clinical Reasoning Engine**

For every case:

**What do you know?**

**What don\'t you know?**

**What is dangerous?**

**What must you exclude?**

**What should you do now?**

**What can wait?**

**When should you escalate?**

**What information would change management?**

This would align extremely well with the GMC\'s stated purpose.

**9. Create a "Why is the other answer wrong?" system**

This is one of the most useful educational features you could add.

Instead of:

Correct answer: C

give:

**A --- Why wrong**

Would be appropriate if\...

**B --- Why wrong**

Tempting because\...

**C --- Correct**

Because\...

**D --- Why wrong**

Would become appropriate if\...

**E --- Why wrong**

The key discriminator is\...

Then:

**Exam trap**

Candidates often choose B because\...

This is much more educational than merely explaining the correct answer.

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

  Pleuritic pain  ↑                          ↓

**25. Your biggest competitor isn\'t actually another Q-bank**

The competitive landscape is increasingly:

**PassMedicine** → volume/reputation\
**Quesmed** → all-in-one ecosystem\
**Pastest** → established question-bank brand\
**Geeky Medics** → free/OSCE strength\
**MedRevisions/UKMLARevisions** → content-map + AI + analytics\
**MLA Prep** → app/offline/flashcards\
**new AI products** → adaptive learning/AI tutors/voice.
([iatroX](https://www.iatrox.com/blog/best-ukmla-question-banks-2026?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

A recent study of medical students also found PassMedicine was the most
frequently used UKMLA resource among respondents, followed by Geeky
Medics, with Quesmed next. ([PubMed Central
(PMC)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13197485/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Therefore:

**Don\'t try to beat PassMedicine at being PassMedicine.**

Don\'t compete primarily on:

**"We have 10,953 questions."**

Compete on:

**"AMaC understands how you perform and tells you exactly how to
improve."**

**32. What I would prioritise**

If you have limited development time, I would **not** build 30 new
features.

I\'d do these in order:

**🔴 PRIORITY 1 --- GMC Content Map engine**

Complete mapping + live syllabus + coverage dashboard.

**🔴 PRIORITY 2 --- Diagnostic + personalised study plan**

"Tell us when your exam is → find your weaknesses → give me today\'s
work."

**🔴 PRIORITY 3 --- Readiness dashboard**

Turn activity into meaningful performance information.

**🔴 PRIORITY 4 --- Weakness Loop**

Every mistake generates targeted learning and re-testing.

**🔴 PRIORITY 5 --- Full AKT simulation**

Realistic timed exam experience + detailed post-exam debrief.

**🔴 PRIORITY 6 --- CPSA performance simulator**

Voice/actor interaction + scoring.

**🟠 PRIORITY 7 --- GMC/GMP professional practice engine**

**🟠 PRIORITY 8 --- Clinical currency/update system**

**🟠 PRIORITY 9 --- F1 transition/on-call simulator**

**🟡 PRIORITY 10 --- Gamification/community/leaderboards**

I would **not** put gamification ahead of the first nine.

**33. The really interesting market gap**

After looking at the current competitors, I think there is a space for
AMaC to own:

**"The clinical performance platform for becoming a safe UK doctor."**

Not simply:

UKMLA Q-bank.

Because the GMC itself describes the MLA as assessing readiness for safe
practice, management of uncertainty and person-centred care. ([General

That gives you a very strong legitimate educational philosophy.

You can then connect:

**UKMLA → CPSA → F1 → clinical practice**

rather than stopping at:

**question → answer → score.**

-   actor traps

-   diagnostic/planning tools.
    ([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html))

The problem is that these currently feel like **a collection of
impressive tools**.

The next stage is to make them feel like **one intelligent system that
takes a candidate from "I don\'t know where I stand" to "I know exactly
what I need to do next."**

That, in my opinion, is the strongest way for AMaC to compete with
PassMedicine/Quesmed/MedRevisions/MLA Prep rather than trying to beat
each of them at their own game.
([iatroX](https://www.iatrox.com/blog/best-ukmla-question-banks-2026?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

If you want, I can take this **one step further and produce a complete
AMaC UKMLA product/website blueprint** --- including the **exact new
homepage structure, dashboard screens, features to build, pricing/free
strategy, SEO pages, candidate journey, GMC compliance wording, and a
competitor-by-competitor gap table**.

Yes. And after a closer look, I would actually be **quite aggressive
about changing parts of the existing AMaC UKMLA page**, because there
are some things that are excellent but currently dilute the strongest
proposition.

The GMC has now made the September 2026 content map the relevant version
for MLA assessments, and it is explicitly a **live document**. It also
frames the MLA around **safe practice, managing uncertainty and holistic
patient-centred care**. ([General Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/education/medical-licensing-assessment/mla-content-map?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

So I would think about AMaC in two parallel tracks:

1.  **What new things could make AMaC exceptional?**

2.  **What should we remove/change because it is confusing, weak,
    outdated or potentially risky?**

**A. MORE IDEAS --- LET\'S REALLY BRAINSTORM**

I\'m going to go beyond the obvious "add AI / add more questions".

**1. The AMaC "What should I do now?" button**

This could appear everywhere.

Candidate opens AMaC and presses:

**What should I do now?**

The system considers:

-   exam date

-   previous performance

-   weak areas

-   unanswered GMC content

-   recent mistakes

-   CPSA performance

-   time available

And gives:

**Your next 35 minutes**

12 questions --- acute medicine\
8 questions --- previously wrong\
5 min --- capacity\
10 min --- CPSA communication

This is extremely sticky.

**2. "Explain it to me like I\'m about to sit the exam"**

Every question could have three explanation levels:

**10-second answer**

**What you need to know**

**60-second explanation**

**Why?**

**Deep dive**

**Why the other options are wrong**

This accommodates candidates who are revising rapidly versus those
learning properly.

**3. The "one-minute medicine" mode**

Candidate has 10 minutes before a lecture / train / lunch.

**Give me 10 minutes of high-yield UKMLA revision.**

AMaC generates:

-   5 questions

-   3 flashcards

-   1 clinical trap

-   1 safety point

-   1 CPSA phrase

Done.

**4. "I keep getting this wrong"**

A button after every incorrect question:

**I still don\'t understand this**

Then AMaC changes teaching method.

For example:

**Question explanation**

→ simple explanation

→ clinical scenario

→ analogy

→ comparison table

→ similar question

→ re-test.

That\'s much better than repeating the same explanation.

**5. Error taxonomy**

This could become one of AMaC\'s strongest features.

Every wrong answer is classified:

**🔵 Knowledge error**

"I didn\'t know it."

**🟡 Recognition error**

"I knew it but didn\'t recognise the presentation."

**🟠 Reasoning error**

"I knew the facts but chose the wrong conclusion."

**🔴 Safety error**

"I chose an unsafe action."

**🟣 Reading error**

"I missed something in the stem."

**⚫ Exam strategy error**

"I changed from the correct answer."

After 500 questions:

**Your biggest problem isn\'t knowledge.**

42% of your errors are clinical reasoning errors.

That\'s enormously useful.

**6. "Change one thing"**

After an incorrect question:

**What single thing would have made you choose correctly?**

Candidate selects:

-   recognise red flag

-   know guideline

-   distinguish diagnoses

-   prioritise safety

-   read stem differently

AMaC then tracks that.

This develops metacognition.

**7. "Same case, different question"**

Excellent UKMLA training.

Example:

**Case**

65-year-old with chest pain.

Then:

**Q1:** Most likely diagnosis?

**Q2:** Most appropriate next investigation?

**Q3:** Initial management?

**Q4:** What complication should concern you?

**Q5:** What would make you escalate?

**Q6:** What should you tell the patient?

Same clinical world, six different decisions.

This trains **clinical reasoning**, not isolated recall.

**8. "The question changed --- did your decision change?"**

Another sophisticated feature.

Example:

Patient has chest pain.

Then reveal:

**New information:**\
BP 82/50.

Candidate must reconsider.

Then:

**New information:**\
ECG shows ST elevation.

Then:

**New information:**\
Patient refuses treatment.

This could train **dynamic clinical reasoning** beautifully.

It also aligns with the GMC emphasis on managing uncertainty. ([General
Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/education/medical-licensing-assessment/mla-content-map?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**9. "Safe answer vs clever answer"**

This could become a trademark.

Sometimes candidates select an intellectually sophisticated answer when
the exam wants the **safe immediate action**.

Show:

**❌ Clever but unsafe**

**✅ Safe and appropriate**

**⭐ Excellent / complete**

This is particularly useful for AKT and CPSA.

**10. "What would an F1 do?"**

After selected questions:

**What would actually happen on a UK ward?**

Example:

You suspect sepsis.

Then:

**Who do you call?**

**What do you document?**

**What do you prescribe?**

**What do you monitor?**

**When do you escalate?**

This bridges exam preparation and actual clinical practice.

**11. The "bleep simulator"**

I still think this could be a killer feature.

**18:42**

**Bleep: Ward 7 --- patient NEWS2 8**

You respond.

Then:

**Bleep: Ward 4 --- K 6.5**

Then:

**Bleep: relative wants to speak to doctor**

Then:

**Bleep: nurse asks you to prescribe insulin**

Candidate has to prioritise.

Then:

**How did you perform?**

Clinical urgency\
Prioritisation\
Escalation\
Communication\
Documentation\
Prescribing safety

That is something few conventional UKMLA resources can replicate.

**12. "Night shift mode"**

Make it realistic.

**You are the FY1 covering 120 patients overnight.**

Every few minutes another problem appears.

The candidate has to:

-   triage

-   delegate

-   escalate

-   assess

-   prescribe

-   handover

Then the next morning:

**Handover**

Candidate gives SBAR for the three sickest patients.

That could eventually become a **post-UKMLA AMaC F1 product**, too.

**13. "Doctor vs examiner" mode**

This is very AMaC.

Candidate answers a CPSA.

Then show:

**What the patient heard**

versus

**What the examiner scored**

versus

**What the candidate thought they communicated**

The mismatch could be fascinating.

**14. "Silence simulator"**

For communication stations.

The system deliberately gives an emotional patient response.

Candidate has to **not fill the silence**.

Then score:

You interrupted after 1.7 seconds.

This is the kind of subtle performance training that can distinguish
AMaC.

**15. "Bad actor / difficult patient" levels**

Current Actor Trap Simulator is a good start.
([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html))

I\'d create:

**Level 1**

Cooperative patient

**Level 2**

Anxious patient

**Level 3**

Angry patient

**Level 4**

Hidden agenda

**Level 5**

Actively challenging patient

**Level 6**

Examiner nightmare

And candidate doesn\'t know which level they\'ve entered.

**16. "Patient agenda detector"**

The candidate should learn:

**What is this patient actually worried about?**

After a station:

Patient\'s stated concern: X\
Patient\'s hidden concern: Y

That teaches ICE much better than memorising "ask ICE".

**17. "Say it naturally"**

This is important.

I would actually reduce reliance on memorised scripts.

Candidate says:

"I would like to acknowledge your concerns and validate your
emotions..."

That may technically sound good but can sound rehearsed.

AMaC could say:

**Too scripted**

Then provide:

"I can see this is really worrying you."

This would reinforce natural UK communication.

**18. Candidate speech analysis**

Eventually:

**Your communication profile**

You:

-   speak too quickly

-   overuse jargon

-   interrupt

-   fail to signpost

-   don\'t check understanding

-   don\'t verbalise safety

-   over-explain

This is incredibly valuable for international candidates.

**19. Accent should not be the target**

I\'d explicitly state:

**AMaC does not train you to lose your accent.**

It trains clarity, natural clinical English and safe communication.

That could be a very attractive and ethical positioning point for
international candidates later.

**20. "UK clinical English" rather than "NHS language"**

I think there is a conceptual distinction here.

Candidates don\'t really need to learn "NHS language".

They need:

**Natural UK clinical communication**

-   how doctors introduce themselves

-   how nurses speak to doctors

-   escalation language

-   referral language

-   documentation language

-   patient-friendly language

-   professional disagreement

-   handover

I\'d broaden this.

**21. A "UK doctor dictionary"**

Not vocabulary like:

haemoglobin = hemoglobin.

More like:

**"I'm not happy with this patient."**

What does that actually mean?

**"Can you review this patient?"**

How urgent is it?

**"I think we should escalate."**

What does a safe escalation sound like?

This is useful for IMGs but also UK graduates.

**22. The "GMC four-domain" dashboard**

This is an obvious opportunity that AMaC doesn\'t currently foreground
enough.

The current Good medical practice framework has four equally important
domains:

1.  Knowledge, skills and development

2.  Patients, partnership and communication

3.  Colleagues, culture and safety

4.  Trust and professionalism. ([General Medical
    Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/professional-standards/good-medical-practice-2024?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

AMaC could show:

**Your professional practice profile**

Knowledge --- 82%\
Patient partnership --- 91%\
Team/safety --- 67%\
Trust/professionalism --- 86%

That is much more current than simply having an "Ethics & Law" resource.

**23. Add "colleague scenarios"**

I think this is underdeveloped.

Examples:

A registrar asks you to do something outside your competence.

You notice a colleague repeatedly making a prescribing error.

A nurse raises a safety concern and the registrar dismisses it.

A colleague makes a discriminatory comment.

You are too unwell to safely work.

The current GMC standards explicitly cover respectful workplaces,
leadership, safe delegation, continuity, responding to safety risks and
professional conduct. ([General Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/professional-standards/good-medical-practice-2024?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

This is fertile UKMLA material.

**24. "What would you do if your senior is wrong?"**

This deserves its own module.

Candidates need to practise:

respectful challenge

escalation

hierarchy

patient safety

documentation

second opinion

That is extremely relevant to UK practice.

**25. "Consent isn\'t just a checkbox"**

Build scenarios where the candidate has to distinguish:

-   consent

-   capacity

-   refusal

-   coercion

-   best interests

-   emergency treatment

-   confidentiality

-   information sharing

Then:

**Why isn\'t this simply an ethics question?**

Because it tests practical safe clinical behaviour.

**26. "Legal ≠ ethical ≠ GMC standard"**

This could be a very high-yield teaching feature.

For each scenario:

**Law says\...**

**GMC says\...**

**Good clinical practice says\...**

**Exam answer\...**

Candidates frequently conflate these.

**27. "Guideline conflict" questions**

This is advanced.

Give:

NICE recommendation A

local hospital practice B

Ask:

What should the candidate do?

Teach candidates how to reason when guidance isn\'t identical.

**28. "Guideline changed" alerts**

Candidate logs in:

🔔 **3 things changed since your last revision**

Example:

GMC content map updated\
NICE recommendation changed\
BNF prescribing update

Then:

**Review the affected questions**

This is a killer retention feature.

**29. "You haven\'t revised this in 42 days"**

Spaced repetition based on actual forgetting.

Not just:

flashcards due.

Instead:

**You\'re at risk of forgetting these 12 topics.**

**30. "Exam confidence" vs actual performance**

Ask:

How confident are you?

Then compare:

Confidence: 92%\
Actual accuracy: 68%

This teaches calibration.

Then later:

Confidence: 82%\
Accuracy: 84%

Candidate becomes better at judging themselves.

That is sophisticated medical education.

**31. "Prediction traps"**

After answering:

**Would you change your answer?**

Record:

-   initial answer

-   final answer

-   whether change helped

Then tell them:

You change correct answers 27% of the time.

That\'s highly actionable exam strategy.

**32. Build a "last 72 hours" system**

Not just Exam Morning Card.

**72 hours before**

No new major topics.

**48 hours**

High-yield weak areas.

**24 hours**

Consolidation.

**Exam morning**

Minimal cognitive load.

**5 minutes before**

Don\'t learn medicine.

This could become:

**AMaC Final 72**

**33. "Don\'t revise everything"**

I would make this a marketing philosophy.

**The final weeks aren\'t about learning everything.**

They\'re about eliminating avoidable mistakes.

That fits your performance positioning beautifully.

**B. NOW --- WHAT I WOULD ACTUALLY CHANGE ON THE CURRENT AMAC PAGE**

This is the important part.

I see several things I\'d amend.

**🔴 1. Change the sentence:**

Current:

**"UKMLA isn\'t about knowing more medicine."**
([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html))

I would **not use that**.

It is punchy, but factually too absolute.

The AKT obviously tests substantial medical knowledge.

And the GMC says the content map sets out the **core knowledge, skills
and behaviours** needed for UK practice. ([General Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/education/medical-licensing-assessment/mla-content-map?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**Better:**

**UKMLA isn\'t only about knowing medicine.**

**It\'s about applying knowledge safely, managing uncertainty and
communicating effectively under pressure.**

That is much harder to criticise.

**🔴 2. Change "UK-trained doctor"**

Current:

"thinking and communicating like a UK-trained doctor under pressure"

I\'d amend this.

It risks sounding like AMaC is teaching candidates to **imitate a
particular identity** rather than demonstrate professional competence.

Better:

**thinking and communicating safely in UK clinical practice**

or:

**applying clinical knowledge and professional skills in the UK
context**

**🔴 3. Change "voice of confidence that passes stations"**

Current wording:

"the voice of confidence that passes stations."
([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html))

I\'d change it.

Confidence isn\'t what passes a station.

It could also imply that performance theatre is more important than
competence.

**Better:**

**clear, safe communication under pressure**

Much stronger.

**🔴 4. "Instant Fail Atlas" needs careful wording**

I actually love the concept.

But:

**Instant Fail Atlas**

could be interpreted as AMaC claiming these behaviours universally cause
an instant fail.

That is potentially too categorical.

I\'d rename:

**Critical Safety Atlas**

or

**High-Risk Station Atlas**

Then each card can say:

**Potential critical error**

rather than:

**instant fail**

unless the specific assessment\'s published marking framework genuinely
supports that exact consequence.

This is one change I\'d make quite urgently.

**🔴 5. "free marks on every station"**

Current:

"Documentation Coach \... free marks on every station."
([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html))

I\'d remove **"free marks"**.

There are no guaranteed marks.

Use:

**A commonly missed opportunity to demonstrate safe documentation.**

or:

**A simple step candidates often forget to verbalise.**

**🔴 6. "Complete UK NHS ranges"**

Current:

"Complete UK NHS ranges" ([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html))

I\'d change this.

There isn\'t necessarily one universal "UK NHS range" for every test.

Ranges can vary by:

-   laboratory

-   assay

-   age

-   sex

-   pregnancy

-   local laboratory practice.

Better:

**Common UK reference ranges and clinically important thresholds**

And explicitly tell candidates:

**Always interpret results using the reference range provided by the
relevant laboratory.**

**🔴 7. "Antibiotic Guide --- first-line antibiotics"**

This needs governance.

First-line antimicrobial choices can change and can vary by:

-   infection

-   patient factors

-   local policy

-   resistance

-   allergy

-   pregnancy

-   renal function.

I\'d change:

**First-line UK antimicrobial choices, with alternatives and key safety
considerations**

And make the **date/review status** visible.

**🔴 8. "DVLA stop durations"**

I would make this much more carefully worded.

Current:

"Stop durations, notify requirements\..."
([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html))

Those are particularly vulnerable to change.

I\'d have:

**DVLA medical standards --- current requirements and notification
rules**

and every item should have:

**Last checked: \[date\]**

**Source: DVLA**

**🔴 9. "NHS Language Coach"**

I\'d probably rename it.

Current:

**NHS Language Coach** ([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html))

It risks sounding a little artificial.

I\'d use:

**UK Clinical Communication Coach**

Then include:

-   patient language

-   colleague language

-   escalation

-   handover

-   documentation

-   referral

-   telephone communication.

Much broader and more valuable.

**🔴 10. "Examiner marking grids and full Fail / Pass / High-performance
transcripts"**

This is potentially one of your strongest features.

But I would clarify:

**AMaC examiner-style marking grids**

unless these are actually based on the specific university\'s validated
assessment criteria.

You don\'t want someone thinking:

"This is the actual GMC examiner mark scheme."

That\'s a trust/compliance issue.

**🔴 11. Be careful with "the standard"**

The page says:

"Written for the AKT paper and the CPSA stations --- the standard, and
how it is actually assessed."
([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html))

I\'d change this.

You don\'t want to imply access to confidential examination material or
official examiner criteria.

Better:

**Written around the GMC MLA framework and the skills candidates need to
demonstrate in the AKT and CPSA.**

The GMC content map is the framework for both components. ([General
Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/education/medical-licensing-assessment/mla-content-map?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**🟠 12. The 429 conditions figure needs changing**

This one is definitely worth fixing.

The page currently says:

**429 conditions and 220 presentations.**
([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html))

But the current GMC map is live and was updated again in September 2026,
including replacing PCOS with PMOS. ([General Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/education/medical-licensing-assessment/mla-content-map?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Therefore I\'d remove the hard-coded number from the marketing headline.

Say:

**Every question is mapped to the current GMC MLA Content Map.**

Then dynamically show the current numbers if you want.

**🟠 13. 10,953 questions is impressive --- but I wouldn\'t make it the
hero**

Keep it.

But don\'t make:

**10,953**

the main reason to buy.

Competitors already compete heavily on volume. PassMedicine is reported
as having 11,000+ questions, while the market increasingly competes on
mapping, explanations, adaptive learning, mocks and OSCE integration.
([iatroX](https://www.iatrox.com/blog/best-ukmla-question-banks-2026?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Your headline should be:

**Know what you need to improve.**

Then:

**10,953+ questions**

as supporting evidence.

**🟠 14. 293 CPSA stations --- same issue**

Keep the number.

But explain what it means.

**293 CPSA stations**

History • communication • acute care • professionalism • examination •
prescribing • data interpretation • telephone

The number itself doesn\'t tell a candidate whether the stations are
good.

**🟠 15. Too many tools are currently presented as equal**

This is probably the biggest UX issue.

You currently have:

-   Say This Avoid This

-   Do This Never Do That

-   Master Cards

-   Flashcards

-   Instant Fail Atlas

-   Examination Coach

-   ECG/ABG

-   DVLA

-   antibiotics

-   ethics

-   normal values

-   prescribing

-   NHS language

-   documentation

-   SBAR

-   frameworks

-   recovery scripts

-   spoken OSCE

-   actor traps

-   study planner

-   route finder

-   diagnostic

-   exam morning card. ([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html))

**This is too much for a new candidate.**

They may think:

"Which one am I supposed to use?"

I would reorganise everything into:

**LEARN**

Knowledge + reference

**PRACTISE**

Questions + flashcards

**PERFORM**

CPSA + voice + actor

**FIX**

Weaknesses + mistakes + recovery

**READY**

Mocks + readiness + exam plan

Then the existing tools sit underneath.

**🟠 16. Don\'t call everything a "tool"**

The word appears repeatedly.

Instead:

**Your UKMLA preparation system**

with **5 pathways**.

This makes AMaC feel like a product rather than a resource library.

**🟠 17. Make the free offer much stronger**

Current:

"Get a free chapter." ([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html))

I\'d change that.

A chapter is not necessarily what a candidate wants.

Offer:

**Take the free AMaC UKMLA Diagnostic**

**25--50 questions**

Then:

Your result:

Cardiology: 72%\
Respiratory: 81%\
Psychiatry: 54%\
Professionalism: 63%

Then:

**See your weak areas**

That creates far more conversion potential.

Competitors are already using free diagnostics as a funnel. ([MLA
Prep](https://www.mlaprep.co.uk/blog/ukmla-question-bank-comparison?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**🟠 18. Add "Try before you buy"**

This is increasingly important.

Competitors explicitly promote free questions/diagnostics. ([MLA
Prep](https://www.mlaprep.co.uk/blog/ukmla-question-bank-comparison?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

AMaC should have:

**Try 10 real AMaC questions --- no card required**

Then:

**Take the 50-question diagnostic**

Then:

**Unlock your personalised plan**

That is a much better acquisition funnel.

**🟢 19. Keep the three AMaC principles**

I actually like:

**Think like an examiner.**\
**Speak like a doctor.**\
**Perform with confidence.**

It\'s memorable.

But I\'d slightly change the third:

**Think like an examiner**

Understand what is being assessed.

**Speak like a doctor**

Communicate clearly, naturally and safely.

**Perform under pressure**

Apply your knowledge when it matters.

That is more defensible and less performance-theatre oriented.

**20. I would introduce a new fourth principle**

**Know where you stand.**

That could become the whole readiness philosophy.

So:

**Think like an examiner.**\
**Speak like a doctor.**\
**Perform under pressure.**\
**Know where you stand.**

Then the fourth is powered by the diagnostic/readiness engine.

**21. One potentially enormous idea: AMaC "Candidate Passport"**

Every candidate gets a persistent:

**UKMLA Candidate Passport**

It records:

**GMC content coverage**

████████░░ 82%

**Knowledge**

█████████░ 91%

**Reasoning**

███████░░░ 72%

**Safety**

█████████░ 94%

**CPSA**

██████░░░░ 63%

**Timing**

███████░░░ 75%

Then:

**Your current priority: clinical reasoning**

Every time they study, their passport changes.

This could become one of the most recognisable AMaC concepts.

**22. And I would make one philosophical change**

Don\'t make AMaC promise:

**"We will help you pass."**

Make the promise:

**"We will show you exactly what you need to improve and train you to
perform safely under UKMLA conditions."**

That is both more credible and more aligned with the GMC framework.

**And one thing I would NOT do**

I would **not simply add another 5,000 questions.**

The market is already crowded with high-volume banks; PassMedicine is
widely recognised for volume, Quesmed for its integrated ecosystem, and
newer competitors are pushing content-map alignment, diagnostics, mocks
and AI.
([iatroX](https://www.iatrox.com/blog/best-ukmla-question-banks-2026?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

AMaC has a much more interesting opportunity:

**Become the platform that diagnoses the candidate.**

Not:

"Here are 10,953 questions."

But:

**"Here is what you are bad at, why you are bad at it, what you need to
do today, and whether you\'ve actually fixed it."**

That is a considerably stronger moat.

And I think the **next thing we should do is inspect AMaC page-by-page
rather than brainstorming further in the abstract**: UKMLA homepage, AKT
bank, CPSA station pages, study tools, clinical references,
pricing/checkout, About, and the individual question/station UX. I can
mark each existing element **KEEP / AMEND / REMOVE / REPLACE / NEW**,
including the actual wording I would change.

Yes. I would go further now and treat the **actual AMaC page as a
product that needs restructuring**, not just adding more features.

The current page is impressive in quantity, but it is trying to sell
**too many things at once**. It currently presents 293 CPSA stations,
10,953 AKT questions, 105 Master Cards, 177 "Say This/Avoid This" cards,
93 "Do This/Never Do That" cards, 12 spoken stations, 75 actor traps,
multiple clinical references, planners and diagnostics.
([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

The competitor problem is real: Quesmed, for example, is now advertising
11,000+ clinical questions, 3,000 basic-science questions, 15,000
flashcards, videos, mocks, AI OSCE voice/text and progress tracking.
([Quesmed](https://quesmed.com/mla-questionbank/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))
So **AMaC cannot win by simply adding more resources.**

I would do the following.

**1. Change the whole architecture of the UKMLA page**

At present it reads like:

**Here are all our resources.**

I would change it to:

**Tell us where you are → AMaC tells you what to do → AMaC trains you →
AMaC shows whether you\'ve improved.**

The page should have five big sections:

**① ASSESS ME**

**Where am I now?**

**② TEACH ME**

**What do I need to know?**

**③ TEST ME**

**Can I apply it?**

**④ TRAIN ME**

**Can I perform it under pressure?**

**⑤ PROVE I\'M READY**

**Am I actually ready for the exam?**

Every existing feature then belongs underneath one of those.

That immediately makes the enormous amount of content much easier to
understand.

**2. Make the Diagnostic the front door**

I would seriously consider replacing:

**Get a free chapter of our UKMLA material**

as the principal CTA.
([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

A chapter is a passive lead magnet.

Instead:

**Take the free AMaC UKMLA Diagnostic**

30 questions.\
15--20 minutes.\
See exactly where your strengths and weaknesses are.

Then:

**Your result**

**Overall: 71%**

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Area**                                 **Performance**
  ---------------------------------------- ------------------------------
  Medicine                                 78%

  Surgery                                  73%

  Paediatrics                              62%

  Psychiatry                               81%

  O&G                                      59%

  Professionalism                          67%

  Clinical reasoning                       61%
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

Then:

**Your biggest opportunity: clinical reasoning**

And:

**Start your personalised AMaC plan**

That is a far stronger conversion mechanism.

MLA Prep is already using a free-question approach to get candidates to
"see where you stand," so this is becoming a competitive expectation.
([MLA
Prep](https://www.mlaprep.co.uk/blog/ukmla-question-bank-comparison?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**3. The new central AMaC concept: "Your UKMLA Profile"**

Every candidate should have this.

**MY UKMLA PROFILE**

**Knowledge**

82%

**Clinical reasoning**

68%

**Patient-centred communication**

91%

**Safety**

86%

**Professionalism**

73%

**Timing**

64%

**CPSA performance**

77%

Then:

**Your 3 priorities**

🔴 Clinical reasoning\
🟠 Timing\
🟠 Professionalism

And:

**Don\'t revise everything equally.**

That sentence could become one of AMaC\'s strongest messages.

**4. Add a "GMC coverage" page**

This should be a **major selling point**, not a small statement.

The GMC says the current content map applies to MLA assessments from
September 2026, and explicitly says it is a **live document** that will
be updated. It provides the framework for both AKT and CPSA. ([General
Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/education/medical-licensing-assessment/mla-content-map?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

So AMaC should have:

**GMC MLA CONTENT MAP**

**Overall coverage**

**94%**

Then:

100% = every current GMC map area has been covered by at least one AMaC
learning item.

Click into:

**Cardiovascular**

→ presentations\
→ conditions\
→ questions\
→ CPSA stations\
→ weak areas

This could be one of your biggest competitive differentiators.

**5. Don\'t just map questions --- map *skills***

This is important.

The GMC doesn\'t describe the MLA simply as a knowledge list. It says
candidates need to demonstrate readiness for **safe practice**, ability
to **manage uncertainty**, and **holistic patient-centred care**.
([General Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/education/medical-licensing-assessment/mla-content-map?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

So every question/station should ideally carry tags such as:

**GMC capability**

-   Safe practice

-   Managing uncertainty

-   Patient-centred care

-   Clinical reasoning

-   Communication

-   Professionalism

-   Teamworking

-   Escalation

Then candidates can practise:

**Give me 20 managing-uncertainty questions.**

That is far more sophisticated than another subject filter.

**6. I would actually REMOVE the word "Ethics & Law" as a major
category**

Not remove the content.

**Reframe it.**

The current GMC framework is much broader than traditional "ethics and
law." Good medical practice now explicitly covers patient partnership,
communication, colleagues, culture, safety, leadership, delegation,
professionalism, conflicts of interest, discrimination and more.
([General Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/professional-standards/good-medical-practice-2024?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

I\'d call the AMaC section:

**Professional Practice & Patient Safety**

Then subcategories:

-   Consent & capacity

-   Confidentiality

-   Safeguarding

-   Professional boundaries

-   Errors & duty of candour

-   Speaking up

-   Teamwork

-   Delegation

-   Discrimination

-   Leadership

-   Conflicts of interest

-   Patient-centred care

-   Fitness to practise

-   Raising concerns

That is much more modern.

**7. Build a GMC "4-domain" mode**

The current Good medical practice framework has four equally important
domains:

1.  Knowledge, skills and development

2.  Patients, partnership and communication

3.  Colleagues, culture and safety

4.  Trust and professionalism. ([General Medical
    Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/professional-standards/good-medical-practice-2024?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

AMaC could mirror this:

**Professional Practice**

**Domain 1**

Knowledge, skills & development

**Domain 2**

Patients, partnership & communication

**Domain 3**

Colleagues, culture & safety

**Domain 4**

Trust & professionalism

This gives AMaC a very credible contemporary framework.

**8. Your "Do This / Never Do That" needs a rethink**

The concept is good.

The **absolute language** is the problem.

The GMC itself says Good medical practice is **not a set of rigid
rules**; doctors must apply professional judgement according to context.
([General Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/professional-standards/the-professional-standards/good-medical-practice/about-good-medical-practice?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Therefore:

**❌ NEVER DO THIS**

can sometimes be educationally misleading.

I\'d use:

**High-risk mistakes**

and:

**Usually unsafe**

**Usually appropriate**

**Depends on context**

**Escalate / seek advice**

This is much closer to real clinical reasoning.

**9. Same issue with "Say This / Avoid This"**

Keep it.

But don\'t make it appear that there is a single magical sentence that
passes.

Change:

**Say This**

to:

**Safe ways to phrase it**

And:

**Avoid This**

to:

**Potentially problematic phrasing**

Then:

**Why it matters**

This avoids teaching rote scripts.

**10. I would make "Recovery Scripts" much bigger**

This is a genuinely interesting AMaC feature.

The current page has 15 recovery scenarios.
([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

I would turn this into:

**CPSA Recovery Engine**

Candidate:

"I\'ve completely forgotten the patient\'s medication..."

AMaC teaches:

**Pause → acknowledge → recover → continue safely**

Other situations:

-   forgot ICE

-   lost your structure

-   forgot a red flag

-   patient becomes angry

-   patient starts crying

-   actor challenges you

-   you give incorrect information

-   you realise you made an unsafe statement

-   you run out of time

-   you don\'t know the answer

-   examiner interrupts

-   patient asks something outside your knowledge

This is very practical.

**11. "I don\'t know" training**

This deserves its own module.

A candidate should learn how to say:

"I\'m not certain, so I would seek senior advice."

versus:

confidently inventing an answer.

That directly fits the GMC\'s **managing uncertainty** theme. ([General
Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/education/medical-licensing-assessment/mla-content-map?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Call it:

**Managing Uncertainty**

Then train:

**What do I know?**

**What don\'t I know?**

**Is there immediate danger?**

**What information do I need?**

**Who should I involve?**

**What is my safety-net?**

This could be a signature AMaC teaching methodology.

**12. Add "Safety-netting simulator"**

Candidate finishes consultation.

AMaC asks:

**What would you tell the patient to look out for?**

Candidate gives answer.

Then scoring:

-   red flags

-   timeframe

-   who to contact

-   emergency escalation

-   understanding

This is useful for both CPSA and actual clinical practice.

**13. Add "Escalation ladder"**

For clinical scenarios:

**Level 1**

Manage yourself

**Level 2**

Discuss with senior

**Level 3**

Urgent senior review

**Level 4**

Emergency response

Candidate chooses.

Then:

**Why?**

This teaches clinical judgement.

**14. Add "Delegation simulator"**

This is particularly attractive because the GMC now explicitly
emphasises **safe delegation** and continuity of care. ([General Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/professional-standards/good-medical-practice-2024?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Example:

You\'re an FY1.

Which should you:

**Do yourself?**

**Delegate?**

**Discuss with registrar?**

**Escalate immediately?**

This is both UKMLA-relevant and F1-relevant.

**15. Add "Speaking up" simulator**

This is another underexploited area.

Example:

You notice a registrar has prescribed the wrong insulin dose.

What do you do?

Then progressively harder:

The registrar becomes defensive.

The ward is busy.

The consultant is unavailable.

The nurse tells you not to make trouble.

This could be excellent.

The GMC specifically says doctors should help create environments where
staff can raise concerns safely and should act promptly when patient
safety is seriously compromised. ([General Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/professional-standards/the-professional-standards/good-medical-practice/the-duties-of-medical-professionals-registered-with-the-gmc?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**16. "Team conflict" simulator**

Examples:

-   nurse disagrees with you

-   registrar dismisses your concern

-   colleague is rude to patient

-   consultant asks you to do something beyond competence

-   colleague appears impaired

-   disagreement over escalation

The candidate needs to balance:

**patient safety + respect + hierarchy + escalation.**

That is much more realistic than traditional ethics MCQs.

**17. Create a "Patient-centredness score"**

This should be measurable.

For CPSA:

**Patient-centredness**

**8.2/10**

Measured through:

-   agenda

-   preferences

-   concerns

-   shared decision-making

-   understanding

-   empathy

-   individual circumstances

-   checking agreement

The GMC explicitly emphasises partnership and not making assumptions
about what patients prefer. ([General Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/professional-standards/good-medical-practice-2024?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**18. Add "clinical context switching"**

One thing real doctors constantly do:

switch between different problems.

AMaC should test this.

Example:

You are dealing with:

**Patient A:** chest pain\
**Patient B:** hypoglycaemia\
**Patient C:** angry relative\
**Patient D:** abnormal blood result

Then:

**Which do you deal with first?**

This is an excellent bridge between UKMLA and F1.

AMaC is building preparation that bridges the transition from medical
student to doctor:

**acute deterioration · prescribing · escalation · handover ·
prioritisation · communication · patient safety**

\[Explore the F1 pathway\]

**Built by doctors. Designed around how candidates actually learn.**

AMaC is independent educational preparation.

It is not affiliated with or endorsed by the GMC.

Its content is developed around publicly available GMC frameworks and
relevant UK clinical guidance.

\[See our Editorial & Clinical Standards\]

This is the direction I would take.

**4. The homepage should NOT show every feature**

This is a big change I would make.

The current page effectively says:

Here are 30 things we have.

For example, the live page lists Master Cards, 1,302 flashcards, 222
Instant Fail Atlas cards, clinical references, examination coaching,
DVLA, antibiotics, ethics, normal values, prescribing, NHS language,
documentation, SBAR, frameworks, recovery scripts, spoken OSCEs, actor
traps, study plans, route finding and diagnostics.
([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html))

That\'s impressive to us.

It can be **overwhelming to a candidate**.

The candidate should see:

**What do you need help with?**

**📚 I need to learn**

AKT

**🧠 I need to improve my reasoning**

Clinical reasoning

**🗣️ I need to practise CPSA**

CPSA

**🔴 I keep failing**

Failure recovery

**⏱️ My exam is soon**

Final sprint

**✅ I want to know if I\'m ready**

Readiness

Then the existing resources sit inside those pathways.

**5. Dashboard --- this should be the heart of AMaC**

I would build the candidate dashboard around this:

**Good morning, Ahmed**

**Your UKMLA readiness**

**78%**

Improving ↑ 6% this month

Then:

**Your performance**

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Area**                                               **Score**
  ------------------------------------------------------ ----------------
  Knowledge                                              84%

  Clinical reasoning                                     71%

  Safety                                                 92%

  Professional practice                                  79%

Then:

**Your biggest weakness**

**Clinical reasoning**

You have made 37 reasoning errors in your last 250 questions.

**Start 20-minute repair session →**

**6. "What should I do today?"**

This should be the biggest button on the dashboard.

**What should I do today?**

AMaC generates:

**15 minutes**

Weak-topic questions

**10 minutes**

Previous errors

**10 minutes**

Spaced repetition

**10 minutes**

CPSA

**5 minutes**

Professional practice

**Total: 50 minutes**

**Start today\'s plan →**

This is where AMaC becomes a **coach rather than a library**.

**7. The GMC map dashboard**

The GMC\'s current map applies to assessments from September 2026 and is
explicitly a live document. ([General Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/education/medical-licensing-assessment/mla-content-map?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Therefore:

**MY GMC MLA MAP**

**Overall coverage: 91%**

Then:

**Presentations**

Chest pain --- 100%\
Breathlessness --- 100%\
Abdominal pain --- 84%\
Collapse --- 72%\
Confusion --- 96%

**Conditions**

ACS --- Mastered\
Heart failure --- Mastered\
PE --- Learning\
AF --- Weak\
Endocarditis --- Not tested

But I\'d go further.

Show:

**Coverage ≠ mastery**

This is critical.

A candidate might have answered 10 AF questions and still be poor at AF.

So:

**Coverage:** 100%

**Mastery:** 63%

That distinction is excellent educationally.

**8. The mastery algorithm**

I\'d define AMaC mastery roughly as:

Candidate must demonstrate:

1.  correct answer

2.  correct answer on a different question

3.  correct application in a different clinical context

4.  delayed recall

5.  no repeated safety error

Then:

**MASTERED**

rather than:

100 questions completed.

This is one of the features I would invest in heavily.

**9. Error dashboard**

This is another major AMaC USP.

**Why are you losing marks?**

**38% --- knowledge gaps**

**24% --- clinical reasoning**

**17% --- missed clue**

**11% --- unsafe decision**

**6% --- timing**

**4% --- changed correct answer**

Then:

**Your problem is not mainly knowledge.**

That\'s incredibly useful.

**10. Candidate "weakness loop"**

Every error creates:

**ERROR**

↓

**WHY?**

↓

**TEACH**

↓

**SIMILAR QUESTION**

↓

**DELAY**

↓

**RETEST**

↓

**MASTER**

I would actually name this:

**AMaC Weakness Loop**

That becomes proprietary product language.

**11. Readiness score --- but with an important caveat**

Yes, build it.

But don\'t claim:

"82% chance of passing."

That would be an unnecessary and potentially problematic claim.

Instead:

**AMaC Readiness Score: 82/100**

And explain:

This is an AMaC learning indicator based on your recent performance,
coverage, mastery, mocks and CPSA practice. It is not a GMC prediction
or guarantee of examination outcome.

This is much safer.

The GMC explicitly says it does not endorse or monitor commercial
preparation courses. ([General Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/registration-and-licensing/join-our-registers/plab/plab-1-guide/what-resources-should-you-use-to-prepare?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**13. Pricing strategy**

This is where I would **not** copy competitors blindly.

The current market is cheap:

-   Quesmed advertises an AKT-only plan at £39.99/year and AKT+CPSA at
    £59.99/year.
    ([Quesmed](https://quesmed.com/mla-questionbank/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

-   UKMLARevisions advertises £25/month, £36/3 months and £49/6 months.
    ([UKMLARevisions](https://www.ukmlarevisions.com/pricing?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

-   MLA Prep advertises £9.99 for one month and £34.99 lifetime. ([MLA
    Prep](https://mlaprep.co.uk/pricing?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

So AMaC shouldn\'t simply charge £100+ because it has lots of content.

**My suggested starting structure:**

**FREE**

**£0**

-   diagnostic

-   20--50 AKT questions

-   small flashcard set

-   GMC map preview

-   limited CPSA station

-   basic performance report

Purpose:

**Prove AMaC is good before asking for money.**

**AKT**

**3 months --- £29.99**

**6 months --- £44.99**

**12 months --- £59.99**

Includes:

-   full AKT bank

-   GMC mapping

-   flashcards

-   mocks

-   analytics

-   personalised plans

-   Weakness Loop

**CPSA**

**3 months --- £34.99**

**6 months --- £49.99**

Includes:

-   293 stations

-   marking frameworks

-   Master Cards

-   communication resources

-   recovery

-   actor traps

-   spoken practice

**COMPLETE UKMLA**

**6 months --- £69.99**

Everything.

This would put AMaC slightly above the cheapest products but still
comfortably within the market.

**14. But I would introduce one unusual pricing option**

**Pass-Date Protection**

Candidate buys:

**6 months**

If their exam date changes, they can extend access once.

This is a very attractive feature because exam dates, medical-school
schedules and preparation timelines can change.

Don\'t promise unlimited extension.

Something like:

**One free extension if your UKMLA/assessment date changes materially.**

This could differentiate AMaC.

**15. Student pricing**

I would strongly consider:

**UK medical student price**

verified university email.

Why?

Because UK students are the natural core audience for UKMLA.

The GMC confirms that UK medical students graduating from UK
universities take the MLA as part of their degree. ([General Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/education/medical-licensing-assessment?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

You also want to penetrate whole cohorts.

**16. University / society licensing**

This is potentially much bigger than individual subscriptions.

Offer:

**AMaC University Cohort**

A medical school or student society gets:

-   cohort dashboard

-   question bank

-   CPSA bank

-   institutional analytics

-   diagnostic

-   mock exams

-   faculty access

-   student progress

But be careful:

**Don\'t provide universities with individual student surveillance
unless there is a legitimate educational/privacy framework and
appropriate consent/governance.**

The commercial product could be:

**Institutional learning analytics**

rather than:

"See exactly how each student is performing."

**17. Student society partnerships**

This could be cheap acquisition.

Offer medical societies:

20% discount code

or:

free diagnostic + society-specific offer.

Then ask societies to run:

**AMaC UKMLA Diagnostic Week**

That gets candidates into the funnel.

**18. Referral system**

Candidate gets:

Invite 3 friends → unlock 30 days of CPSA/AI practice.

Not:

3 friends = free lifetime access.

Keep it controlled.

**19. Do NOT compete on price**

This is important.

If MLA Prep can sell lifetime access for £34.99, trying to undercut them
becomes a race to the bottom. ([MLA
Prep](https://mlaprep.co.uk/pricing?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

AMaC should say:

**You aren\'t buying a question bank. You\'re buying a preparation
system.**

Then demonstrate the difference.

So don\'t build:

Build:

**21. AMaC\'s moat**

I would define the moat as:

**Candidate performance data**

The more a candidate uses AMaC, the more AMaC knows:

-   what they know

-   what they forget

-   what they misunderstand

-   what traps them

-   how they reason

-   how they communicate

-   how they perform under time

-   where they make safety errors

Then the platform becomes increasingly personalised.

A competitor can copy:

293 stations.

It\'s much harder to copy:

**your entire longitudinal learning profile.**

**22. The AI strategy**

I would **not** build:

**"Ask AMaC anything"**

That\'s generic and easy to copy.

Instead:

**AMaC Clinical Coach**

It should say:

"You\'ve made four errors in capacity questions. Let\'s identify the
underlying problem."

Or:

"You know the diagnostic criteria but repeatedly choose the wrong next
step. Let\'s practise clinical decision-making."

Or:

"Your CPSA scores are good except when the patient becomes emotional.
Let\'s practise that."

That is **personalised AI**, not generic AI.

**23. AI should never invent clinical guidance**

This is particularly important for a medical education platform.

The AI should preferentially answer from:

-   AMaC-approved educational content

-   GMC

-   NICE

-   BNF

-   other approved authoritative sources

and identify when guidance is uncertain/context-dependent.

Every AI clinical answer should ideally show:

**Source / review date**

That becomes a major trust feature.

**24. Clinical governance**

I would create an actual:

**AMaC Clinical Editorial Board**

Even if initially small.

For each question:

**Author**

Doctor / educator

**Clinical reviewer**

Doctor

**Editorial review**

Question quality

**Reference check**

Guideline/source

**Last reviewed**

Date

**Next review**

Date

**Version**

v2.1

Then:

**Report a problem**

on every question.

This is particularly important because the GMC describes its own MLA
content map as a live document and expects it to reflect day-to-day
medical practice. ([General Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/education/medical-licensing-assessment/mla-content-map?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**25. Create an AMaC correction policy**

This could be public:

**If we identify a clinically significant error, we review the affected
content, correct it, and record the change internally. Material changes
may trigger re-review of related questions.**

Then:

**Recently updated**

Question 1827\
Updated: October 2026\
Reason: guidance change

That is powerful.

**26. Build a GMC Content Map monitoring process**

This should be a real internal workflow.

**Weekly automated check**

GMC MLA page

↓

detect change

↓

flag affected AMaC content

↓

clinical review

↓

amend

↓

version

↓

notify candidates where appropriate

The current GMC map has already changed in September 2026, including the
replacement of PCOS with PMOS, demonstrating why this cannot be treated
as a static syllabus. ([General Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/education/medical-licensing-assessment/mla-content-map?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**27. Do the same for NICE/BNF/DVLA**

Don\'t say:

"Everything is always up to date."

Instead:

**Guidance monitored and reviewed**

with visible timestamps.

This is more credible.

**28. The GMC compliance language I would use**

This is important.

**USE**

**Aligned with the current GMC MLA Content Map**

**Mapped to the GMC MLA Content Map**

**Built around the GMC framework for the MLA**

**Designed to support preparation for the AKT and CPSA**

**Uses GMC Good medical practice as a professional standards reference**

The GMC says the content map provides the framework for the AKT and
CPSA. ([General Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/education/medical-licensing-assessment/mla-content-map?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**DON\'T USE**

GMC-approved

GMC-endorsed

GMC-certified

Official GMC preparation

GMC-approved questions

Actual GMC exam questions

Questions based on recalled GMC exam questions

Guaranteed GMC pass

The GMC explicitly says it does not endorse or monitor commercial
preparation courses, and warns candidates about courses claiming to
provide GMC exam content. ([General Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/registration-and-licensing/join-our-registers/plab/plab-1-guide/what-resources-should-you-use-to-prepare?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

This is one area where I would be **very strict**.

**29. One wording change I would make immediately**

Current:

**"UKMLA isn\'t about knowing more medicine."**
([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html))

Change to:

**"UKMLA isn\'t only about knowing medicine. It\'s about applying
knowledge safely, managing uncertainty and caring for patients
effectively."**

Why?

Because the GMC explicitly describes the MLA as testing core knowledge,
skills and behaviours and identifies those three themes. ([General
Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/education/medical-licensing-assessment?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**30. Another immediate wording change**

Current:

**"thinking and communicating like a UK-trained doctor"**
([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html))

Change to:

**"thinking, communicating and making safe clinical decisions in UK
practice."**

Much better.

**31. Change "free marks"**

Current:

**"Documentation Coach \... free marks on every station."**
([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html))

Remove that.

Use:

**"A commonly missed opportunity to demonstrate safe, clear
documentation."**

No claim of guaranteed marks.

**32. Change "Instant Fail Atlas"**

I would probably rename it:

**Critical Safety Atlas**

Then cards can have:

**Critical safety issue**

**Why it matters**

**What the candidate should do**

**What to say**

**What to avoid**

**Examiner perspective**

This is safer than claiming an error automatically means "instant fail."

**33. Change "Never"**

This applies to:

**Do This, Never Do That**

I would rename:

**Do This --- Avoid This**

or:

**Safe Practice --- Common Pitfalls**

Because Good medical practice is not simply a rigid checklist; the GMC
explicitly says doctors must apply professional judgement according to
context. ([General Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/professional-standards/the-professional-standards/good-medical-practice/about-good-medical-practice?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

**34. Change the "429 conditions" marketing**

This is now particularly important.

The current AMaC page says:

**429 conditions and 220 presentations.**
([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html))

But the current GMC map is live and has already been amended in
September 2026. ([General Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/education/medical-licensing-assessment/mla-content-map?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

I would replace the sentence entirely:

**Every AMaC question is mapped to the current GMC MLA Content Map, so
you can see exactly what you\'ve covered and where your gaps remain.**

If you want the number, pull it dynamically from your mapping database.

**35. Don\'t call normal values "complete UK NHS ranges"**

The current page says:

**"Complete UK NHS ranges."**
([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html))

I\'d change to:

**Common UK reference ranges and clinically important thresholds**

and add:

**Reference ranges may vary between laboratories and patient groups;
always use the range supplied by the relevant laboratory where
provided.**

That\'s medically safer.

**36. Antibiotics needs stronger context**

Current:

**"First-line antibiotics\..."**
([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html))

I\'d use:

**UK antimicrobial choices, alternatives and key safety considerations**

and show:

**Source:** NICE / BNF / relevant guidance\
**Reviewed:** date

Because antimicrobial recommendations are context-sensitive.

Current:

**"Stop durations, notify requirements\..."**

This is important because this is information candidates could

**40. CPSA AI --- don\'t just copy Quesmed**

Quesmed already has unlimited AI voice/text OSCE with 340+ AI stations
and says its marking is benchmarked against practising doctors.

AMaC should therefore differentiate through:

**41. The "Actor Trap" is potentially a major USP**

The current page has 5 actor-trap stations and 75 trap cards.
([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html))

I would expand this substantially.

**Hidden Agenda Engine**

The candidate doesn\'t know:

-   what the patient is hiding

-   what they are worried about

-   what they will challenge

-   which red flag they will mention casually

Then AMaC analyses whether the candidate discovered it.

That\'s genuinely good CPSA training.

**42. "Recovery" could become another USP**

Most platforms teach:

perfect station.

AMaC can teach:

**what happens when you mess up.**

That is realistic.

The candidate:

forgets ICE

AMaC:

**Recover without panicking.**

Candidate:

gets emotional patient.

AMaC:

**Recover the consultation.**

Candidate:

runs out of time.

AMaC:

**Prioritise and close safely.**

This is extremely marketable.

**43. The F1 bridge is bigger than I initially thought**

The 2026 Foundation Programme curriculum has now been revised, with
stronger emphasis on generalist practice, patient safety, inclusivity
and sustainability. ([UK Foundation
Programme](https://foundationprogramme.nhs.uk/curriculum/uk-fp-curriculum/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

The current F1/F2 framework includes capabilities around:

-   clinical assessment

-   clinical prioritisation

-   holistic planning

-   communication

-   continuity

-   teamwork

-   speaking up

-   ethics/law

-   professional development. ([UK Foundation
    Programme](https://foundationprogramme.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2024/04/FP_Curr_Oct22_v7.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

That means AMaC\'s proposed:

**UKMLA → F1**

isn\'t just a commercial idea.

There is a very natural educational progression.

**72. My final strategic verdict**

If I were advising AMaC as a business, I would **not** say:

"You need more questions."

You already have **10,953** and **293 CPSA stations**.
([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html))

I would say:

**You need to make those resources intelligent.**

The market is already moving toward:

**questions → analytics → AI → readiness → voice**

as shown by Quesmed, MLA Prep and UKMLARevisions.
([Quesmed](https://quesmed.com/mla-questionbank/?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

AMaC\'s opportunity is to go one step beyond:

**Candidate → diagnosis → personalised learning → performance → mastery
→ readiness → F1**

And there is a particularly strong strategic reason to do that now: the
GMC\'s current MLA framework explicitly centres **safe practice,
uncertainty and person-centred care**, while the newly revised 2026
Foundation Programme curriculum strengthens the bridge toward patient
safety, generalist practice, teamwork and professional capability.
([General Medical
Council](https://www.gmc-uk.org/education/medical-licensing-assessment?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

So my proposed AMaC identity would ultimately be:

**AMaC**

**Prepare. Perform. Practise safely.**

**The intelligent UK medical exam and clinical performance platform.**

That is a much bigger and more defensible proposition than **"another
UKMLA question bank."**

Yes. I've now compared the suggestions in your document with the
**current AMaC UKMLA page** and the **current GMC MLA position**. My
conclusion is that the document is directionally very good, but I would
make some important changes to the proposed strategy before you start
building.

The current GMC position is particularly important: the MLA has an **AKT
and CPSA**, and the current content map applies to assessments from
**September 2026 onward**. The GMC explicitly describes the purpose as
demonstrating readiness for safe practice, managing uncertainty and
holistic patient-centred care, and says the map is a live document.
([GMC
UK](https://www.gmc-uk.org/education/medical-licensing-assessment/mla-content-map?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

Your document recognises this very well.

**My overall verdict**

**AMaC\'s underlying product: very strong**

**Current UKMLA website/product presentation: needs substantial
restructuring**

**The document\'s proposed direction: about 85--90% right**

**What I would actually implement: a more focused version**

The biggest mistake would be to take the document and turn **every idea
into a feature**.

You would end up with an even bigger AMaC.

The goal should be the opposite:

**Make AMaC feel simpler to use while making it much more intelligent
underneath.**

Your current page already has **293 CPSA stations and 10,953 AKT
questions**, plus a large collection of communication, reference,
planning and performance resources.
([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

The problem isn\'t lack of content.

It\'s that a new candidate can still ask:

**"What exactly should I do when I join AMaC?"**

That is the problem I would solve first.

**1. The biggest change I recommend**

I agree strongly with the document\'s idea of moving from:

**"Here are our resources."**

to:

**"Tell us where you are → we\'ll tell you what to do → we\'ll train you
→ we\'ll show you whether you\'ve improved."**

The document calls this the candidate journey.

I would make this the **entire architecture of UKMLA**.

**The five AMaC stages**

**1. ASSESS**

Where am I now?

Diagnostic + baseline.

**2. LEARN**

What do I need to know?

Questions, notes, flashcards, clinical references.

**3. PRACTISE**

Can I apply it?

SBAs, clinical reasoning, uncertainty, next-best-step.

**4. PERFORM**

Can I demonstrate it under pressure?

CPSA, spoken practice, actor simulator, communication.

**5. PROVE**

Have I actually improved enough?

Mocks, weakness repair, readiness.

This is much better than exposing 25 different tools in the first few
seconds.

**2. I would make the Diagnostic the front door**

This is probably the **highest-value immediate change**.

The current page offers:

"Get a free chapter of our UKMLA material"

But your competitors are increasingly using free questions/diagnostics
as acquisition tools. MLA Prep, for example, currently promotes free
UKMLA questions as a way for candidates to assess where they stand.
([MLA
Prep](https://www.mlaprep.co.uk/blog/ukmla-question-bank-comparison?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

I would change AMaC to:

**FREE UKMLA DIAGNOSTIC**

**30 questions · 15--20 minutes**

Find out where you stand before you start revising.

Then show something like:

**Your AMaC UKMLA Profile**

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Area**                                    **Performance**
  ------------------------------------------- ---------------------------
  Medicine                                    78%

  Surgery                                     73%

  Paediatrics                                 62%

  Psychiatry                                  81%

  O&G                                         59%

  Professional practice                       67%

  Clinical reasoning                          61%
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

Then:

**Your biggest opportunity**

🔴 **Clinical reasoning**

You know more medicine than your score currently shows. Your main
weakness is choosing the safest next step.

**\[Build my study plan\]**

That is an infinitely better sales mechanism than:

"Here is a free chapter."

**3. The real AMaC USP should be the AMaC Profile**

I agree strongly with the document here.

But I would simplify it.

Don\'t create 15 different scores.

Have one central dashboard:

**MY UKMLA PROFILE**

**Knowledge**

82%

**Clinical reasoning**

68%

91%

This is the feature that makes AMaC feel like a **system rather than a
question bank**.

The document\'s proposed "What should I do now?" concept is one of the
best ideas in the entire project.

**4. But I would NOT make "Readiness 82%" too prominent initially**

This is one place where I\'d modify the document.

A single:

**UKMLA readiness: 82%**

looks attractive.

But it creates a difficult question:

**82% readiness according to what?**

And worse:

Does 82% mean I have an 82% chance of passing?

You absolutely don\'t want candidates interpreting it that way.

The document itself recognises this caveat.

I would initially call it:

**AMaC Readiness Index**

and explicitly state:

**An AMaC learning indicator based on your activity and performance. It
is not a prediction or guarantee of examination outcome.**

Even better, make the primary output:

**You\'re strongest in:**

Patient-centred communication

**Your biggest gap:**

Clinical reasoning

**Your current priority:**

Next-best-step questions

That is more educationally meaningful than pretending we can predict the
GMC exam.

Therefore simply saying:

"Mapped to the GMC"

is no longer enough.

AMaC needs to **show it**.

This is critical.

**THE UK LICENSING STANDARD**

and later:

**8. I would definitely amend the current hero wording**

The current page says:

"UKMLA isn\'t about knowing more medicine."

I agree completely with the document that this should go.

The AKT clearly tests medical knowledge.

I\'d use:

**The UKMLA isn\'t only about knowing medicine.**

Apply knowledge safely. Manage uncertainty. Communicate effectively.

Current concept:

"thinking and communicating like a UK-trained doctor under pressure"

I would not use it.

Instead:

You\'re not trying to teach someone to **imitate a UK doctor**.

You\'re teaching them to demonstrate the expected clinical and
professional behaviours.

**17. Another excellent idea: "same case, different question"**

I\'d definitely build this eventually.

Example:

**ONE PATIENT --- SIX DECISIONS**

65-year-old with chest pain.

**Q1:** Most likely diagnosis?

**Q2:** Most appropriate investigation?

**Q3:** Initial management?

That is genuine clinical reasoning.

towards:

**18. Dynamic cases are even better**

This is one of the strongest longer-term ideas.

Candidate sees:

Chest pain.

They make a decision.

Then:

BP 82/50.

What now?

Then:

ECG shows ST elevation.

What now?

Then:

Patient refuses treatment.

What now?

This directly trains the candidate to **update decisions when the
clinical situation changes**.

And it fits very naturally with the GMC\'s emphasis on managing
uncertainty. ([GMC
UK](https://www.gmc-uk.org/education/medical-licensing-assessment/mla-content-map?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

↓

**20. I would NOT simply copy competitors\' AI**

So:

isn\'t enough.

This is where I think AMaC can potentially create something genuinely

After the candidate speaks:

**AMaC PERFORMANCE REPORT**

**Communication:** 8/10\
**Clinical reasoning:** 6/10\
**Safety:** 9/10\
**Patient-centredness:** 8/10\
**Structure:** 7/10\
**Timing:** 5/10

**You missed**

-   empathy

-   signposting

-   some jargon

-   interrupted once

-   did not explicitly check understanding

**Your next exercise**

Repeat the same station with a more emotionally distressed patient.

**31. And I would make one thing the ultimate AMaC concept**

I think the document gets very close to this, but I would sharpen it.

**AMaC Intelligence**

Not necessarily as a product name visible everywhere.

But as the technology underneath the platform.

AMaC continuously learns:

**What you know**

↓

**What you forget**

↓

**What you get wrong**

↓

**Why you get it wrong**

↓

**How you perform under time**

↓

**How you communicate**

↓

**Where you make safety errors**

↓

**What you should practise next**

↓

**Whether you improved**

That is the moat.

A competitor can copy:

10,953 questions.

They can copy:

293 stations.

They can copy:

AI tutor.

They cannot easily copy a **longitudinal candidate performance model**
built from thousands of interactions.

The document identifies this as AMaC\'s potential moat, and I agree.

Call Bleep Cards and planned simulators.

So AMaC has an unusually good opportunity:

**UKMLA**

**Prepare safely**

↓

**F1**

**Practise safely**

↓

**Clinical performance**

That creates a much bigger AMaC ecosystem than a single examination
product.

But **UKMLA must first become excellent**.

**My final recommendation**

If this were my project, I would **not redesign AMaC around "more
content."**

I\'d redesign it around this:

**AMaC tells you what you need to improve --- then trains you until you
improve it.**

And underneath that:

**GMC blueprint → Diagnostic → Candidate Profile → Personalised plan →
Questions → Weakness Loop → CPSA performance → Mock → Readiness**

Everything else becomes supporting material.

The current GMC framework gives you an unusually good foundation for
this because it explicitly centres **safe practice, uncertainty and
holistic patient-centred care**. ([GMC
UK](https://www.gmc-uk.org/education/medical-licensing-assessment/mla-content-map?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

And importantly, the current AMaC site already contains many of the
ingredients needed to make this work; the challenge is **integration and
positioning**, not starting from scratch.
([AMaC](https://amac-medical.com/ukmla.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com))

We should now stop brainstorming and do the **actual AMaC UKMLA rebuild
page-by-page**.

WORDING → WHY → GMC/clinical/commercial issue → priority**

Then we can produce the **complete new UKMLA homepage, section by
section, with the exact copy you can give to your web developer**,
followed by the dashboard and candidate journey.

Yes. The next step is to turn the strategy into an **actual AMaC UKMLA
